choosing-your-honey.title: Forest Multi-Floral or Tulsi Infused: Picking Your Honey – Naadu Nalam
choosing-your-honey.meta_description: Two honeys, two very different jobs in the kitchen. A short guide to telling them apart and using them well.
headings: Forest Multi-Floral or Tulsi Infused: Picking Your Honey
content: Forest Multi-Floral or Tulsi Infused: Picking Your Honey

We stock two honeys, and they are not interchangeable. One is a broad forest harvest; the other is built around tulsi. Knowing which is which saves you from using the interesting one where it will be wasted.

Bees foraging across mixed forest flowering produce a darker, deeper honey whose character shifts a little with each harvest. That variation is the nature of a multi-floral crop, not a defect. It is the one to reach for when honey is doing the heavy lifting: drizzled over curd, stirred into warm water, or spread plainly on bread.

Lighter in body with a distinct herbal note running through it. It works best where you want that note to register — in tea, in a morning tonic, or taken on its own by the spoon. Bury it in a heavily spiced dish and you will not taste what you paid for.

Raw honey sets over time, particularly in cooler months. Granules at the bottom of the jar are a sign it has not been heat-treated into permanent clarity. Stand the jar in warm water for a few minutes and it loosens again. Avoid boiling it.
Both keep well in a sealed jar at room temperature. Use a dry spoon — water introduced into the jar is the main thing that shortens honey’s life.

cold-pressed-vs-refined-oils.title: Cold-Pressed vs Refined: Why Our Oils Taste Like the Seed – Naadu Nalam
cold-pressed-vs-refined-oils.meta_description: Cold-pressed sesame and groundnut oil carry flavour and colour that refining strips out. Here is the difference.
headings: Cold-Pressed vs Refined: Why Our Oils Taste Like the Seed
content: Cold-Pressed vs Refined: Why Our Oils Taste Like the Seed

Open a bottle of cold-pressed sesame oil next to a refined one and the difference is immediate. One smells like toasted seed; the other smells like almost nothing. That gap is the whole argument for pressing cold.

The seed is crushed slowly, without added heat. Because temperatures stay low, the aromatic compounds and natural colour survive the process. Refining runs hotter and uses further steps to neutralise and deodorise the oil, which produces a clear, long-lasting, largely flavourless product.

Cold-pressed oils have a lower smoke point, so they are happier at moderate heat than in a hard deep-fry. Our sesame oil suits tempering, rice mixes and pickles, where its flavour is the point. Groundnut oil is the more neutral of the two and handles everyday sautéing comfortably.

Keep the bottle capped, away from the stove, and out of direct light. Cold-pressed oil has not been stripped of the compounds that make it taste good, which also means it does not sit indefinitely. Buy the size you will actually finish in a couple of months.
A sediment layer at the bottom is normal and not a fault. Tip the bottle gently before pouring.

cooking-country-vegetables.title: Drumstick, Snake Gourd and Cluster Beans, Cooked Simply – Naadu Nalam
cooking-country-vegetables.meta_description: Three country vegetables that reward restraint. Minimal handling, short cooking, and very little in the pan.
headings: Drumstick, Snake Gourd and Cluster Beans, Cooked Simply
content: Drumstick, Snake Gourd and Cluster Beans, Cooked Simply
The vegetables that move fastest through our stalls are also the ones people are least sure how to cook. All three below are better treated plainly than dressed up.

Cut the pods into finger-length pieces and leave the tough skin on — you scrape the soft interior out at the table. Drumstick’s flavour is released by simmering, which is why it belongs in sambar and in thin, tamarind-sour gravies rather than in a dry fry. Add it early enough to soften but not so early that it collapses.

Split it lengthways, scrape out the spongy core and the seeds, then slice into half-moons. It holds a great deal of water, so it wants a hot pan and no lid — covered, it stews in its own liquid and turns grey. A quick poriyal with mustard seed, urad dal and grated coconut is all it needs.

The most assertive of the three, with a bitterness that is the point rather than a flaw. Top, tail and chop, then either blanch briefly before frying or cook them long and slow with tamarind. Undercooked cluster beans are unpleasantly squeaky; give them longer than instinct suggests.
None of these keep especially well once cut. Buy what you will cook within two or three days and store them dry, not in a sealed bag.

headings: Many Sellers, One Basket: How Buying Direct Works Here
content: Many Sellers, One Basket: How Buying Direct Works Here
Naadu Nalam is built as a marketplace rather than a single shop. Independent growers and small producers each keep their own store page, and your basket can draw from several of them at once.

Most produce reaches a city through layers that erase where it came from. We take the opposite approach: every listing belongs to a seller with a page you can open. If a batch of drumstick or a jar of forest honey is good, you can go back to the same person for the next one.

A typical order might combine cluster beans from one grower, cold-pressed sesame oil from a small mill, and cardamom from a spice seller. You pay once. Behind the scenes each seller is notified for their own part of the order, which is why items occasionally arrive in more than one packet.

Smaller producers cannot promise the same crate every week of the year, and we would rather show an honest gap than pad the catalogue. When something is out of season it leaves the shelf until it is genuinely ready again.
If you are new here, the simplest place to start is a small mixed order: a vegetable or two, one pantry staple, and one thing you have not cooked with before.

privacy-policy.title: Privacy Policy – Naadu Nalam
content: Your privacy matters to us. This Privacy Policy explains how Naadu Nalam collects, uses, stores and protects information when you use our website and services. It applies to this website and to orders fulfilled through it.
Order information — your name, delivery address, pin code, email address and phone number, collected at checkout so we can process, pack, deliver and invoice your order.
Account information — if you create an account, your username, email address and saved delivery addresses.
Enquiry information — the name, email address and message you submit through our contact form.
Technical information — your IP address, browser type and pages viewed, recorded in standard server logs and used to keep the site secure and working correctly.
To process, pack and deliver your order, and to contact you about it.
To handle refunds, replacements and delivery issues under our Refund Policy.
To respond to enquiries you send us.
To manage your account, where you have created one.
To keep records required for tax and accounting purposes.
To detect and prevent fraud and misuse of the website.
We send marketing email only if you have asked us to. Every marketing email includes an unsubscribe link, and unsubscribing does not affect order-related messages.
We do not collect or store your card, UPI or net-banking details.
Where an online payment method is offered, payment is completed on the payment provider’s own secure systems and we receive only a confirmation of the result.
Where you choose Cash on Delivery, payment is collected at the time your order is handed to you.
We use cookies that are necessary for the site to function, including keeping items in your cart and keeping you signed in.
Most browsers let you block or delete cookies through their settings. Please note that blocking necessary cookies may stop parts of the website, such as the cart and checkout, from working correctly.
We share your information only where it is needed to run the service:
Delivery partners — your name, address and phone number, so your order can be delivered.
Sellers on our marketplace — where an item is supplied by an independent seller, the details needed to prepare and dispatch that item.
Payment providers — where you pay online, to process and verify the transaction.
Our hosting and IT providers — who store and process data on our behalf under contract.
Authorities — where we are required to disclose information by law.
We do not sell your personal information, and we do not share it for third-party advertising.
This website is served over an encrypted HTTPS connection. Access to order and customer data is limited to people who need it to fulfil orders and support customers.
No method of transmission or storage is completely secure, but we take reasonable steps to protect your information against loss, misuse and unauthorised access.
Order and invoice records are retained for as long as required under applicable tax and accounting rules.
Account details are kept until you ask us to delete your account.
Contact-form enquiries are kept only as long as needed to deal with the enquiry.
Under India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, you may ask us to:
Confirm what personal data we hold about you and obtain a copy of it.
Correct data that is inaccurate, incomplete or out of date.
Erase your personal data, where we are not required to retain it.
Withdraw a consent you previously gave, at any time.
Nominate another person to exercise these rights on your behalf.
To make a request, write to us using the contact details below. We will respond within a reasonable period.
This website is not directed at children, and we do not knowingly collect personal data from anyone under 18. Orders should be placed by an adult.

If you have a concern about how your personal data has been handled, contact our grievance officer at hello@naadunalam.in or +91 90921 14630, marking your message for the attention of the Grievance Officer.
If you are not satisfied with our response, you may escalate the matter to the Data Protection Board of India.
We may update this policy as our services change or as the law requires. The current version is always the one published on this page.

headings: Ragi Flour: The Millet Tamil Kitchens Never Gave Up
content: Ragi Flour: The Millet Tamil Kitchens Never Gave Up
Ragi never really left South Indian kitchens. While polished grains took over city shelves, finger millet held its place in porridge, in kali, and in the flat breads people grew up on.

The easiest introduction is a thin porridge. Whisk a couple of spoons of ragi flour into cold water first — always cold, or it will seize into lumps — then cook it out over a low flame, stirring, until it thickens and loses its raw smell. Finish it savoury with buttermilk, salt and shallot, or sweet with a little jaggery.

Ragi has no gluten, so a dough made from it alone will not stretch. Pat it out by hand rather than rolling, or cut it with wheat flour if you want something more forgiving. A one-to-two ratio of ragi to wheat gives you the colour and flavour without fighting the dough.

It is a whole grain with a good deal of fibre, and it is filling in a way that lasts — which is the practical reason it survives as a breakfast and as a first food for children. Nothing exotic; just a grain that does its job.
Store the flour in an airtight jar. Whole-grain flours carry their natural oils and go stale faster than refined ones, so buy in quantities you will get through.

headings: Red Rice or Sona Masoori: Matching the Grain to the Meal
content: Red Rice or Sona Masoori: Matching the Grain to the Meal
Our two most-ordered grains sit at opposite ends of the same shelf. Sona masoori is the light, familiar daily rice. Red rice is heavier, nuttier and keeps its bran. They suit different meals.

A short, soft grain that cooks quickly and stays fluffy. It is the right choice when the rice is a backdrop — under sambar, rasam or a coconut-heavy curry — because it absorbs without turning claggy. Rinse until the water runs mostly clear, then cook with roughly two parts water to one part rice.

Because the bran layer stays on, red rice takes longer, drinks more water, and arrives with a firm bite and a faintly earthy flavour. Soak it for thirty minutes if you can, use closer to two and a half parts water, and give it time. It stands up to strong, sour and spiced dishes that would flatten a softer grain.

Plenty of households keep both and alternate — red rice on days when the meal is simple and the rice should be interesting, sona masoori when the curry is the star. If you are moving toward whole grains, blending the two in the same pot is an easier transition than switching outright, though you will need to soak the red rice first so they finish together.

content: Seasonal Picks: What the Fruit Stalls Have Right Now
Fruit is the part of the catalogue that changes most, because it has to. Here is what our growers are sending in at the moment and what to look for in each.

Judge it by smell and give, not colour — a fruit can look ready and still be firm at the stone. Alphonso arrives slightly under-ripe by design so it survives the journey. Leave it out of the fridge, in paper, until it yields to light pressure at the shoulder, then chill it if you like it cold.

Firmer and starchier than a table banana, which is exactly why it fries well. Green Nendran is for chips and for cooking; wait for real yellow if you want to eat it raw. It ripens happily on the counter and does not need any help.

Guava is ready when the skin shifts from hard green toward pale yellow and the fruit smells sweet from a distance. Papaya is the one most people cut too early — wait for the skin to turn substantially yellow-orange and to soften under the thumb. Both go into the fridge once cut, not before.
Because these come from small growers, availability moves week to week. If something is not on the shelf, it usually means it is not good enough to send yet.

headings: Whole Spices, Ground at Home: Cumin, Coriander, Cardamom
content: Whole Spices, Ground at Home: Cumin, Coriander, Cardamom

We list our spices whole rather than ground, and it is not for the sake of tradition. A spice’s aroma lives in volatile oils held inside the seed. Break the seed and those oils start leaving immediately.

Cumin and coriander both improve with a short dry roast in a pan over a low flame — no oil, constant movement, and off the heat the moment they smell nutty. Let them cool completely before grinding, or the residual heat turns the powder pasty. Grind only what the week needs.

Green cardamom is the clearest case for buying whole: the pod is a sealed container, and cardamom powder goes flat faster than almost anything else in the rack. Crack the pod and use the seeds. Cloves are strong enough that a whole one dropped into rice or a gravy does the work without grinding at all.

Airtight, opaque if you can, and nowhere near the stove. Heat and light are what degrade spice, not time alone — a jar of whole cumin kept properly will outlast a packet of ground cumin several times over.
If you buy one grinder for this, a small hand mill or a dedicated spice jar for your mixer is plenty. It does not need to be elaborate.

cold-pressed-vs-refined-oils.title: Cold-Pressed vs Refined: Why Our Oils Taste Like the Seed
cold-pressed-vs-refined-oils.meta_desc: Cold-pressed sesame and groundnut oil carry flavour and colour that refining strips out. Here is the difference.
body: Cold-Pressed vs Refined: Why Our Oils Taste Like the Seed

Open a bottle of cold-pressed sesame oil next to a refined one and the difference is immediate. One smells like toasted seed; the other smells like almost nothing. That gap is the whole argument for pressing cold.
What cold-pressing actually means

The seed is crushed slowly, without added heat. Because temperatures stay low, the aromatic compounds and natural colour survive the process. Refining runs hotter and uses further steps to neutralise and deodorise the oil, which produces a clear, long-lasting, largely flavourless product.
Cooking with it

Cold-pressed oils have a lower smoke point, so they are happier at moderate heat than in a hard deep-fry. Our sesame oil suits tempering, rice mixes and pickles, where its flavour is the point. Groundnut oil is the more neutral of the two and handles everyday sautéing comfortably.
Storage

Keep the bottle capped, away from the stove, and out of direct light. Cold-pressed oil has not been stripped of the compounds that make it taste good, which also means it does not sit indefinitely. Buy the size you will actually finish in a couple of months.
A sediment layer at the bottom is normal and not a fault. Tip the bottle gently before pouring.

body: Forest Multi-Floral or Tulsi Infused: Picking Your Honey

We stock two honeys, and they are not interchangeable. One is a broad forest harvest; the other is built around tulsi. Knowing which is which saves you from using the interesting one where it will be wasted.
Forest multi-floral

Bees foraging across mixed forest flowering produce a darker, deeper honey whose character shifts a little with each harvest. That variation is the nature of a multi-floral crop, not a defect. It is the one to reach for when honey is doing the heavy lifting: drizzled over curd, stirred into warm water, or spread plainly on bread.
Tulsi infused

Lighter in body with a distinct herbal note running through it. It works best where you want that note to register — in tea, in a morning tonic, or taken on its own by the spoon. Bury it in a heavily spiced dish and you will not taste what you paid for.
On crystallisation

Raw honey sets over time, particularly in cooler months. Granules at the bottom of the jar are a sign it has not been heat-treated into permanent clarity. Stand the jar in warm water for a few minutes and it loosens again. Avoid boiling it.
Both keep well in a sealed jar at room temperature. Use a dry spoon — water introduced into the jar is the main thing that shortens honey’s life.

body: Ragi Flour: The Millet Tamil Kitchens Never Gave Up
Ragi never really left South Indian kitchens. While polished grains took over city shelves, finger millet held its place in porridge, in kali, and in the flat breads people grew up on.
Start with kanji

The easiest introduction is a thin porridge. Whisk a couple of spoons of ragi flour into cold water first — always cold, or it will seize into lumps — then cook it out over a low flame, stirring, until it thickens and loses its raw smell. Finish it savoury with buttermilk, salt and shallot, or sweet with a little jaggery.
Ragi in flatbread

Ragi has no gluten, so a dough made from it alone will not stretch. Pat it out by hand rather than rolling, or cut it with wheat flour if you want something more forgiving. A one-to-two ratio of ragi to wheat gives you the colour and flavour without fighting the dough.
Why people keep it around

It is a whole grain with a good deal of fibre, and it is filling in a way that lasts — which is the practical reason it survives as a breakfast and as a first food for children. Nothing exotic; just a grain that does its job.
Store the flour in an airtight jar. Whole-grain flours carry their natural oils and go stale faster than refined ones, so buy in quantities you will get through.

cooking-country-vegetables.title: Drumstick, Snake Gourd and Cluster Beans, Cooked Simply
cooking-country-vegetables.meta_desc: Three country vegetables that reward restraint. Minimal handling, short cooking, and very little in the pan.
body: Drumstick, Snake Gourd and Cluster Beans, Cooked Simply
The vegetables that move fastest through our stalls are also the ones people are least sure how to cook. All three below are better treated plainly than dressed up.
Drumstick

Cut the pods into finger-length pieces and leave the tough skin on — you scrape the soft interior out at the table. Drumstick’s flavour is released by simmering, which is why it belongs in sambar and in thin, tamarind-sour gravies rather than in a dry fry. Add it early enough to soften but not so early that it collapses.
Snake gourd

Split it lengthways, scrape out the spongy core and the seeds, then slice into half-moons. It holds a great deal of water, so it wants a hot pan and no lid — covered, it stews in its own liquid and turns grey. A quick poriyal with mustard seed, urad dal and grated coconut is all it needs.
Cluster beans

The most assertive of the three, with a bitterness that is the point rather than a flaw. Top, tail and chop, then either blanch briefly before frying or cook them long and slow with tamarind. Undercooked cluster beans are unpleasantly squeaky; give them longer than instinct suggests.
None of these keep especially well once cut. Buy what you will cook within two or three days and store them dry, not in a sealed bag.

whole-spices-ground-at-home.title: Whole Spices, Ground at Home: Cumin, Coriander, Cardamom
whole-spices-ground-at-home.meta_desc: Pre-ground spice loses its oils within weeks. Buying whole costs nothing extra in effort and changes the food.
body: Whole Spices, Ground at Home: Cumin, Coriander, Cardamom

We list our spices whole rather than ground, and it is not for the sake of tradition. A spice’s aroma lives in volatile oils held inside the seed. Break the seed and those oils start leaving immediately.
Dry-roast, then grind

Cumin and coriander both improve with a short dry roast in a pan over a low flame — no oil, constant movement, and off the heat the moment they smell nutty. Let them cool completely before grinding, or the residual heat turns the powder pasty. Grind only what the week needs.
Cardamom and cloves

Green cardamom is the clearest case for buying whole: the pod is a sealed container, and cardamom powder goes flat faster than almost anything else in the rack. Crack the pod and use the seeds. Cloves are strong enough that a whole one dropped into rice or a gravy does the work without grinding at all.
Storing them

Airtight, opaque if you can, and nowhere near the stove. Heat and light are what degrade spice, not time alone — a jar of whole cumin kept properly will outlast a packet of ground cumin several times over.
If you buy one grinder for this, a small hand mill or a dedicated spice jar for your mixer is plenty. It does not need to be elaborate.

seasonal-picks-fruit-stalls.title: Seasonal Picks: What the Fruit Stalls Have Right Now
seasonal-picks-fruit-stalls.meta_desc: Alphonso mango, Nendran banana, pink guava and papaya — what to look for and how to ripen each at home.
body: Seasonal Picks: What the Fruit Stalls Have Right Now
Fruit is the part of the catalogue that changes most, because it has to. Here is what our growers are sending in at the moment and what to look for in each.
Alphonso mango

Judge it by smell and give, not colour — a fruit can look ready and still be firm at the stone. Alphonso arrives slightly under-ripe by design so it survives the journey. Leave it out of the fridge, in paper, until it yields to light pressure at the shoulder, then chill it if you like it cold.
Nendran banana

Firmer and starchier than a table banana, which is exactly why it fries well. Green Nendran is for chips and for cooking; wait for real yellow if you want to eat it raw. It ripens happily on the counter and does not need any help.
Pink guava and papaya

Guava is ready when the skin shifts from hard green toward pale yellow and the fruit smells sweet from a distance. Papaya is the one most people cut too early — wait for the skin to turn substantially yellow-orange and to soften under the thumb. Both go into the fridge once cut, not before.
Because these come from small growers, availability moves week to week. If something is not on the shelf, it usually means it is not good enough to send yet.
